Question 3
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[uv2u2+2v].

a
The critical points lie on the line v=0 and on the hyperbola v2−u2.
b
The critical points lie on the lines u=−2v and u=v.
c
The critical points lie on the parabola u=v2.
d
The critical points lie on the line u=2v.
e
The critical points lie on the line v=0 and on the parabola v=2u2.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=uv2 and y(u,v)=u2+2v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=v2∂x∂v=2uv∂y∂u=2u∂y∂v=2

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|v22uv2u2|=v2⋅2−2uv⋅2u=2v2−4u2v.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=02v2−4u2v=0v(2v−4u2)=0.

The equation v(2v−4u2)=0 defines the line v=0, i.e., the u-axis, and the parabola v=2u2 in the uv-plane.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\ 3xy\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}$ and $v(x,y)=3xy.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =3y & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\ 3y & 3x\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot 3x-(-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}})\cdot 3y \\  & =\frac{9x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =9\cdot \frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =9u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9u}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[xy23xy].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
3v
b
1u
c
uv
d
vu
e
19u
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=xy2 and v(x,y)=3xy.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=1y2∂u∂y=−2xy3∂v∂x=3y∂v∂y=3x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|1y2−2xy33y3x|=1y2⋅3x−(−2xy3)⋅3y=9xy2=9⋅xy2=9u.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=19u

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}$ and $v(x,y)=3xy.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =3y & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\ 3y & 3x\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot 3x-(-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}})\cdot 3y \\  & =\frac{9x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =9\cdot \frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =9u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9u}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[xy23xy].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
3v
b
1u
c
uv
d
vu
e
19u
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=xy2 and v(x,y)=3xy.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=1y2∂u∂y=−2xy3∂v∂x=3y∂v∂y=3x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|1y2−2xy33y3x|=1y2⋅3x−(−2xy3)⋅3y=9xy2=9⋅xy2=9u.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=19u

solution.reasoning: The Jacobian determinant of T⁻¹ is (1/y²)(3x)−(−2x/y³)(3y)=9x/y²=9u. At non-critical points, the determinant of T is its reciprocal, 1/(9u), so choice e is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer-key evidence is provided.

The function $f(x),$ whose graph is shown above, has a stationary point at $x=2$ and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=3.$  By considering the points indicated in the diagram, determine which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem.

I. $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$

II. ${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$

III. The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$
question.worked_solution:
The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:

*If $f:U\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U,$ then*

- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*

- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*

- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* 

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\,.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed,

- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and

- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\ne 0.$

Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$

- Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

- Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. The function f satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at x=1. Indeed,

    • f is continuously differentiable on an open set containing x=1, for example, (0,2), and

    • the derivative of f is nonzero at x=1, i.e., f′(1)≠0.

    Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, f is invertible in some neighborhood of x=1.

  • Statement II is false. Notice that y=−2=f(2). However, the function f does not satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at x=2 since f′(2)=0. So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

  • Statement III is false. Notice that y=2.91=f(3), but f is not continuous at x=3. So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

solution.reasoning: I holds: the graph has nonzero slope at x=1, and f is continuously differentiable nearby, so the inverse function theorem guarantees a local inverse. II is not guaranteed: f′(2)=0, and the local minimum prevents invertibility in any neighborhood of x=2. III is invalid: the graph is discontinuous at x=3, so f′(3) does not exist and the inverse derivative formula does not apply. Thus I only is mathematically correct. questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A bank account had an **initial balance** of $$0.$ During the day, there was a **deposit** of $$20.$ Then there was a **withdrawal** of $$20$ later.
What is the resulting amount in the account?
questions.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- During the day, the account had a *deposit of* $$20,$ which is a change of $+$20.$

- Later, the account had a *withdrawal of* $$20,$ which is a change of $-$20.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0:$

$$
20+(-20)=0
$$

Therefore, the balance returns to its original value of $$0.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The temperature inside an oven **dropped by** ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$ when the door was opened. Then it **rose by** ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$ when the door was closed.

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The temperature is now lower than the initial value.

II. The temperature returned to the initial value.

III. The temperature is now larger than the initial value.
questions.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- When the door was opened, the temperature *dropped by* ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$, which is a change of $-{25}^{∘}\,\text{C}.$

- When the door was closed, the temperature *rose by* ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C},$ which is a change of $+{25}^{∘}\,\text{C}.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0:$

$$
-25+25=0
$$

This means the *total temperature change* is ${0}^{∘}\,\text{C},$ so the temperature returns to its original value.

So, statements I and III are false, while statement II is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
A drone’s elevation **rose by** $85\text{ m}$ while flying up to a roof. Then it **dropped by** $85\text{ m}$ while descending back to the pilot.
Which of the following statements are true?

I. The drone's elevation is now higher than the initial elevation.

II. The drone returned to the initial elevation.

III. The drone's elevation is now lower than the initial elevation.
questions.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- While flying up to a roof, the drone’s elevation *rose by* $85\text{ m}$, which is a change of $+85\text{ m}.$

- While descending back to the pilot, the drone’s elevation *dropped by* $85\text{ m},$ which is a change of $-85\text{ m}.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0:$

$$
85+(-85)=0
$$

This means the *total elevation change* is $0\text{ m},$ so the drone returns to the original elevation.

So, statements I and III are false, while statement II is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Let $x=-5$ and $y=8.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $x+y?$
questions.worked_solution:
The value of $x+y$ is the number located a distance $|y|$ from $x$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $y$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $y$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $x=-5$ on the number line.

- Here, $y=8$, so the distance we move is $|y|=8.$

- Because $y$ is *positive*, we move $8$ units to the *right* from $-5.$

This point corresponds to the number

$$
-5+8=3.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Let $u=4$ and $v=-9.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $u+v?$
questions.worked_solution:
The value of $u+v$ is the number located a distance $|v|$ from $u$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $v$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $v$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $u=4$ on the number line.

- Here, $v=-9$, so the distance we move is $|v|=9.$

- Because $v$ is *negative*, we move $9$ units to the *left* from $4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152428/assets/79c5200c6f0089f7b6cf6be0eec8b97de3ff3a3daa270bfa6e7ae0c480b134f5.png)

This point corresponds to the number

$$
4+(-9)=-5.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Adding Opposite Quantities
canonical_examples.problem:
A drone’s elevation **dropped by** $85\text{ m}$ while descending into a valley. Then it **rose by** $85\text{ m}$ while flying back up.
Which of the following statements are true?

I. The drone’s elevation is now higher than the initial elevation.

II. The drone’s elevation is now lower than the initial elevation.

III. The drone returned to the initial elevation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- While descending, the drone’s elevation *dropped by* $85\text{ m}$, which is a change of $-85\text{ m}.$

- While climbing back up, the drone’s elevation *rose by* $85\text{ m},$ which is a change of $+85\text{ m}.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0{:}$

$$
-85 + 85 = 0
$$

This means the *total elevation change* is $0\text{ m},$ so the drone returns to the original elevation.

So, statements I and II are false, while statement III is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

canonical_examples.problem: Let $p=-3$ and $q=8.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $p+q?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The value of $p+q$ is the number located a distance $|q|$ from $p$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $q$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $q$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $p = -3$ on the number line.

- Here, $q = 8$, so the distance we move is $|q| = 8.$

- Because $q$ is *positive*, we move $8$ units to the *right* from $-3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152428/assets/b44a40ef3278f0b31899b7a98695a92e332859b5d0f7badb82a241b1bcbef022.png)

This point corresponds to the number

$$
-3 + 8 = 5.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
On a number line, a number and its *additive inverse* are at the same distance from zero but on opposite sides. Remember that the distance of a number from zero is given by its *absolute value*.

For instance, the only two numbers that are at a distance of $4$ from zero are $4$ and $-4.$ So, $-4$ is the additive inverse of $4$ (and vice versa).

tutorials.name: Addition and Absolute Values on the Number Line
tutorials.problem:
Now, let $p=6$ and $q=-9.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $p+q?$

The value of $p+q$ is the number located a distance $|q|$ from $p$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $q$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $q$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $p = 6$ on the number line.

- Here, $q = -9$, so the distance we move is $|q| = 9.$

- Because $q$ is *negative*, we move $9$ units to the *left* from $6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152428/assets/265469a65efa2ae63d794ee2ad0eeb79c6754ab18a7bec3791b8ba05007a744e.png)

This point corresponds to the number

$$
6 + (-9) = -3.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let x=−5 and y=8. What point on the number line corresponds to x+y?

a
It's the number −3 located 8 units to the right of −5.
b
It's the number 3 located 8 units to the left of −5.
c
It's the number 3 located 5 units to the right of 8.
d
It's the number −3 located 8 units to the left of −5.
e
It's the number 3 located 8 units to the right of −5.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of x+y is the number located a distance |y| from x on the number line,

  • moving to the right if y is positive, and

  • moving to the left if y is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at x=−5 on the number line.

  • Here, y=8, so the distance we move is |y|=8.

  • Because y is positive, we move 8 units to the right from −5.

This point corresponds to the number −5+8=3.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let p=1 and q=−6. What point on the number line corresponds to p+q?

a
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the right of 1.
b
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
c
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the right of 1
d
It's the number −5 located 1 unit to the right of 6.
e
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The value of p+q is the number located a distance |q| from p on the number line,

  • moving to the right if q is positive, and

  • moving to the left if q is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at p=1 on the number line.

  • Here, q=−6, so the distance we move is |q|=6.

  • Because q is negative, we move 6 units to the left from 1.

This point corresponds to the number 1+(−6)=−5.

question.html:
Question 9
?

Let u=4 and v=−9. What point on the number line corresponds to u+v?

a
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
b
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
c
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
d
It's the number −5 located 4 units to the right of 9.
e
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of u+v is the number located a distance |v| from u on the number line,

  • moving to the right if v is positive, and

  • moving to the left if v is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at u=4 on the number line.

  • Here, v=−9, so the distance we move is |v|=9.

  • Because v is negative, we move 9 units to the left from 4.

This point corresponds to the number 4+(−9)=−5.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
A bank account had an **initial balance** of $$0.$ During the day, there was a **deposit** of $$20.$ Then there was a **withdrawal** of $$20$ later.
What is the resulting amount in the account?
question.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- During the day, the account had a *deposit of* $$20,$ which is a change of $+$20.$

- Later, the account had a *withdrawal of* $$20,$ which is a change of $-$20.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0:$

$$
20+(-20)=0
$$

Therefore, the balance returns to its original value of $$0.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
The temperature inside an oven **dropped by** ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$ when the door was opened. Then it **rose by** ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$ when the door was closed.

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The temperature is now lower than the initial value.

II. The temperature returned to the initial value.

III. The temperature is now larger than the initial value.
question.worked_solution:
In our situation:

- When the door was opened, the temperature *dropped by* ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C}$, which is a change of $-{25}^{∘}\,\text{C}.$

- When the door was closed, the temperature *rose by* ${25}^{∘}\,\text{C},$ which is a change of $+{25}^{∘}\,\text{C}.$

These two changes are *opposite quantities*. When opposite quantities combine, they make $0:$

$$
-25+25=0
$$

This means the *total temperature change* is ${0}^{∘}\,\text{C},$ so the temperature returns to its original value.

So, statements I and III are false, while statement II is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

A drone’s elevation rose by 85 m while flying up to a roof. Then it dropped by 85 m while descending back to the pilot. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The drone's elevation is now higher than the initial elevation.
  2. The drone returned to the initial elevation.
  3. The drone's elevation is now lower than the initial elevation.
a
None
b
II only
c
I and II only
d
III only
e
I only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In our situation:

  • While flying up to a roof, the drone’s elevation rose by 85 m, which is a change of +85 m.

  • While descending back to the pilot, the drone’s elevation dropped by 85 m, which is a change of −85 m.

These two changes are opposite quantities. When opposite quantities combine, they make 0: 85+(−85)=0

This means the total elevation change is 0 m, so the drone returns to the original elevation.

So, statements I and III are false, while statement II is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Let $x=-5$ and $y=8.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $x+y?$
question.worked_solution:
The value of $x+y$ is the number located a distance $|y|$ from $x$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $y$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $y$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $x=-5$ on the number line.

- Here, $y=8$, so the distance we move is $|y|=8.$

- Because $y$ is *positive*, we move $8$ units to the *right* from $-5.$

This point corresponds to the number

$$
-5+8=3.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let x=−5 and y=8. What point on the number line corresponds to x+y?

a
It's the number −3 located 8 units to the right of −5.
b
It's the number 3 located 8 units to the left of −5.
c
It's the number 3 located 5 units to the right of 8.
d
It's the number −3 located 8 units to the left of −5.
e
It's the number 3 located 8 units to the right of −5.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of x+y is the number located a distance |y| from x on the number line,

  • moving to the right if y is positive, and

  • moving to the left if y is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at x=−5 on the number line.

  • Here, y=8, so the distance we move is |y|=8.

  • Because y is positive, we move 8 units to the right from −5.

This point corresponds to the number −5+8=3.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let p=1 and q=−6. What point on the number line corresponds to p+q?

a
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the right of 1.
b
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
c
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the right of 1
d
It's the number −5 located 1 unit to the right of 6.
e
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The value of p+q is the number located a distance |q| from p on the number line,

  • moving to the right if q is positive, and

  • moving to the left if q is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at p=1 on the number line.

  • Here, q=−6, so the distance we move is |q|=6.

  • Because q is negative, we move 6 units to the left from 1.

This point corresponds to the number 1+(−6)=−5.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let p=1 and q=−6. What point on the number line corresponds to p+q?

a
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the right of 1.
b
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
c
It's the number 5 located 6 units to the right of 1
d
It's the number −5 located 1 unit to the right of 6.
e
It's the number −5 located 6 units to the left of 1.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The value of p+q is the number located a distance |q| from p on the number line,

  • moving to the right if q is positive, and

  • moving to the left if q is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at p=1 on the number line.

  • Here, q=−6, so the distance we move is |q|=6.

  • Because q is negative, we move 6 units to the left from 1.

This point corresponds to the number 1+(−6)=−5.
question.knowledge_point: Interpreting Addition Using Absolute Value

solution.reasoning: The sum is 1 + (-6) = -5. Adding -6 moves six units to the left from 1, so option e is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example uses different values.

answers.correct_value: It's the number $-5$ located $6$ units to the left of $1.$
answers.wrong_value: It's the number $5$ located $6$ units to the right of $1$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Let p=−6 and q=9. What point on the number line corresponds to p+q?

a
It's the number 3 located 6 units to the right of 9.
b
It's the number 3 located 9 units to the right of −6.
c
It's the number 3 located 9 units to the left of −6.
d
It's the number −3 located 9 units to the left of −6.
e
It's the number −3 located 9 units to the right of −6.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of p+q is the number located a distance |q| from p on the number line,

  • moving to the right if q is positive, and

  • moving to the left if q is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at p=−6 on the number line.

  • Here, q=9, so the distance we move is |q|=9.

  • Because q is positive, we move 9 units to the right from −6.

This point corresponds to the number −6+9=3.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Let p=−6 and q=9. What point on the number line corresponds to p+q?

a
It's the number 3 located 6 units to the right of 9.
b
It's the number 3 located 9 units to the right of −6.
c
It's the number 3 located 9 units to the left of −6.
d
It's the number −3 located 9 units to the left of −6.
e
It's the number −3 located 9 units to the right of −6.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of p+q is the number located a distance |q| from p on the number line,

  • moving to the right if q is positive, and

  • moving to the left if q is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at p=−6 on the number line.

  • Here, q=9, so the distance we move is |q|=9.

  • Because q is positive, we move 9 units to the right from −6.

This point corresponds to the number −6+9=3.
question.knowledge_point: Interpreting Addition Using Absolute Value

solution.reasoning: The sum is -6 + 9 = 3. Adding positive 9 moves nine units to the right from -6, so option b is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example uses different values.

answers.wrong_value: It's the number $-3$ located $9$ units to the left of $-6.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Let u=4 and v=−9. What point on the number line corresponds to u+v?

a
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
b
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
c
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
d
It's the number −5 located 4 units to the right of 9.
e
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of u+v is the number located a distance |v| from u on the number line,

  • moving to the right if v is positive, and

  • moving to the left if v is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at u=4 on the number line.

  • Here, v=−9, so the distance we move is |v|=9.

  • Because v is negative, we move 9 units to the left from 4.

This point corresponds to the number 4+(−9)=−5.

question.html:
Question 9
?

Let u=4 and v=−9. What point on the number line corresponds to u+v?

a
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
b
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
c
It's the number −5 located 9 units to the left of 4.
d
It's the number −5 located 4 units to the right of 9.
e
It's the number 5 located 9 units to the right of 4.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The value of u+v is the number located a distance |v| from u on the number line,

  • moving to the right if v is positive, and

  • moving to the left if v is negative.

In our situation:

  • We start at u=4 on the number line.

  • Here, v=−9, so the distance we move is |v|=9.

  • Because v is negative, we move 9 units to the left from 4.

This point corresponds to the number 4+(−9)=−5.
question.knowledge_point: Interpreting Addition Using Absolute Value

solution.reasoning: The sum is 4 + (-9) = -5. Adding -9 moves nine units to the left from 4, so option c is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example uses different values.

answers.correct_value: It's the number $-5$ located $9$ units to the left of $4.$
answers.wrong_value: It's the number $5$ located $9$ units to the right of $4.$

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: Let $u=4$ and $v=-9.$ What point on the number line corresponds to $u+v?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The value of $u+v$ is the number located a distance $|v|$ from $u$ on the number line, 

- moving to the *right* if $v$ is *positive*, and

- moving to the *left* if $v$ is *negative*.

In our situation:

- We start at $u=4$ on the number line.

- Here, $v=-9$, so the distance we move is $|v|=9.$

- Because $v$ is *negative*, we move $9$ units to the *left* from $4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14152428/assets/79c5200c6f0089f7b6cf6be0eec8b97de3ff3a3daa270bfa6e7ae0c480b134f5.png)

This point corresponds to the number

$$
4+(-9)=-5.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡3t & 0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡3t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =⟨0-0,-(-{cos}^{2}⁡3t-{sin}^{2}⁡3t),0-0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \sqrt{3} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨({sin}^{2}⁡t-(-{cos}^{2}⁡t)),-(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-0),(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨1,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),-(0+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),(3{sin}^{2}⁡t+3{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,2t,0⟩, \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,2t,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2t & 0 \\ -2t & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 2t \\ -2t & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0-0,-(0-0),1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0,0,1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩, \\ N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(0) & =T(0)\times N(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨(0-1),-(0-(-1)),(1-(-1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-1,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=3,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩, \\ N(3) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(3) & =T(3)\times N(3) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨(-9-16),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨-25,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=2$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,1,2⟩, \\ N(2) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,2,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(2) & =T(2)\times N(2) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,1,2⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨(-1-4),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-5,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=1,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,2,1⟩, \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}⟨-4,5,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(1) & =T(1)\times N(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,2,1⟩\times \frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}⟨-4,5,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{9\sqrt{5}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 5 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{9\sqrt{5}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\sqrt{5}}⟨(-4-5),-(-4-(-4)),(10-(-8))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{9\sqrt{5}}⟨-9,0,18⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨3,5,4⟩, \\ N(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =T(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\times N(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨3,5,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨(-15-0),-(-9-16),(0-20)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨-15,25,-20⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨-3,5,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡5t,\,-1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡5t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡5t+25{cos}^{2}⁡5t} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩}{(\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}})}=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡5t,\,-1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -1 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡5t-0,-({cos}^{2}⁡5t+{sin}^{2}⁡5t),0-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡5t,\,-1,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨({sin}^{2}⁡t-(-{cos}^{2}⁡t)),-(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-0),(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{5{e}^{2t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(2{e}^{t})^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-5{e}^{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}+25{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-5{e}^{2t}-1,-(-10{e}^{2t}-2),2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,2(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)-{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)),0-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),\,1,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
questions.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,\frac{4t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(5)^{2}+(-4t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{25+16{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{20{t}^{2}+25} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩}{(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,2,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2t & -1 \\ 5 & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 5 & -4t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨4t-4t,-(4{t}^{2}+5),-8{t}^{2}-10⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨0,\,-(4{t}^{2}+5),\,-2(4{t}^{2}+5)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}⟨0,t,4⟩, \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}⟨0,4,-t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}⟨0,t,4⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+16}}⟨0,4,-t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+16}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & t & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & -t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+16}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}t & 4 \\ 4 & -t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & -t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & t \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+16}⟨(-{t}^{2}-16),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+16}⟨-({t}^{2}+16),0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}T(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩, \\ N(\pi ) & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t).

$$

$$

Example: 
                    Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,2,\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $\mathbf N(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $\mathbf{N}(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡4t+16{sin}^{2}⁡4t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡4t+{sin}^{2}⁡4t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize $\mathbf T'(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩}{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,2,\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡4t & 2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t & 2 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡4t-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡4t-{cos}^{2}⁡4t),0-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,1,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
The **binormal vector** to a curve $C$ defined by the vector-valued function $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is defined as

$$
\mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \times \mathbf{N}(t),
$$

where $\mathbf{T}$ and $\mathbf{N}$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal vectors, respectively.

The diagram below shows the binormal vector to a curve at some point $P$ on the curve. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14161646/assets/95a892eb30b26d1255d29dcaaac552663443c00b2db6fe1e9168a77be061f2c0.png)

Since $\mathbf B = \mathbf T\times \mathbf N,$ we can conclude that $\mathbf B$ is perpendicular to both $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N,$ and it's pointing downward.

Also, since $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular *unit* vectors, it follows that $\mathbf B$ is also a unit vector.

\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩, \\ N(t) & =⟨0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \sqrt{3} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨({sin}^{2}⁡t-(-{cos}^{2}⁡t)),-(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-0),(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨1,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=12⟨3,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩,N(t)=⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 12⟨1,3sin⁡t,−3cos⁡t⟩
b
 12⟨−3sin⁡t,1,−3cos⁡t⟩
c
 13⟨0,3sin⁡t,3cos⁡t⟩
d
 ⟨0,sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩
e
 12⟨1,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have

B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=12⟨3,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩×⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩=12ijk3−sin⁡tcos⁡t0−cos⁡t−sin⁡t=12[ −sin⁡tcos⁡t−cos⁡t−sin⁡ti−3cos⁡t0−sin⁡tj+3−sin⁡t0−cos⁡tk ]=12⟨(sin2⁡t−(−cos2⁡t)),−(−3sin⁡t−0),(−3cos⁡t−0)⟩=12⟨1,3sin⁡t,−3cos⁡t⟩.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),-(0+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),(3{sin}^{2}⁡t+3{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,1⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 1 \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),-(0+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),(3{sin}^{2}⁡t+3{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that T(t)=110⟨−3sin⁡t,3cos⁡t,1⟩,N(t)=⟨−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t,0⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
110⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t,3⟩
b
110⟨−3cos⁡t,−3sin⁡t,1⟩
c
15⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t,1⟩
d
12⟨−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t,3⟩
e
12⟨sin⁡t,cos⁡t,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=110⟨−3sin⁡t,3cos⁡t,1⟩×⟨−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t,0⟩=110ijk−3sin⁡t3cos⁡t1−cos⁡t−sin⁡t0=110[ 3cos⁡t1−sin⁡t0i−−3sin⁡t1−cos⁡t0j+−3sin⁡t3cos⁡t−cos⁡t−sin⁡tk ]=110⟨(0+sin⁡t),−(0+cos⁡t),(3sin2⁡t+3cos2⁡t)⟩=110⟨sin⁡t,−cos⁡t,3⟩.

question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}⟨{t}^{2},\sqrt{2}t,1⟩, \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}({t}^{2}+1)}⟨2t,\sqrt{2}(1-{t}^{2}),-2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

Question 4
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that T(t)=1t2+1⟨t2,2t,1⟩,N(t)=12(t2+1)⟨2t,2(1−t2),−2t⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
1t2+1⟨−1,2t,−t2⟩
b
1t2+1⟨−2t,t2,1⟩
c
12t2+1⟨−2t,1,0⟩
d
1t2+1⟨t2,0,1⟩
e
1t2+2⟨0,2,t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=1t2+1⟨t2,2t,1⟩×12(t2+1)⟨2t,2(1−t2),−2t⟩=12(t2+1)2ijkt22t12t2(1−t2)−2t=12(t2+1)2[ 2t12(1−t2)−2ti−t212t−2tj+t22t2t2(1−t2)k ]=12(t2+1)2⟨−22t2−2(1−t2),−(−2t3−2t),(2t2(1−t2)−22t2)⟩=12(t2+1)2⟨−2t2−2,2t3+2t,−2t4−2t2⟩=12(t2+1)2⟨−2(t2+1),2t(t2+1),−2t2(t2+1)⟩=1t2+1⟨−1,2t,−t2⟩.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,2t,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2t & 0 \\ -2t & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 2t \\ -2t & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0-0,-(0-0),1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0,0,1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,2t,0⟩, \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨1,2t,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}}⟨-2t,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2t & 0 \\ -2t & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 2t \\ -2t & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0-0,-(0-0),1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+4{t}^{2}}⟨0,0,1+4{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that T(t)=11+4t2⟨1,2t,0⟩,N(t)=11+4t2⟨−2t,1,0⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 12⟨1,0,1⟩
b
 ⟨0,0,1⟩
c
 11+4t2⟨0,0,t⟩
d
 12⟨2,1,1⟩
e
 11+4t2⟨−1,0,2t⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=11+4t2⟨1,2t,0⟩×11+4t2⟨−2t,1,0⟩=11+4t2ijk12t0−2t10=11+4t2[ 2t010i−10−2t0j+12t−2t1k ]=11+4t2⟨0−0,−(0−0),1+4t2⟩=11+4t2⟨0,0,1+4t2⟩=⟨0,0,1⟩.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\pi ) & =T(\pi )\times N(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨(0-0),-(0-4),(0-(-3))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point $t=\pi$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩, \\ N(\pi ) & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\pi ) & =T(\pi )\times N(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨(0-0),-(0-4),(0-(-3))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(0) & =T(0)\times N(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨(0-1),-(0-(-1)),(1-(-1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-1,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩, \\ N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(0) & =T(0)\times N(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,1,1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨(0-1),-(0-(-1)),(1-(-1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨-1,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at the point t=0, given that

T(0)=13⟨1,1,1⟩,N(0)=12⟨−1,1,0⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 16⟨1,2,1⟩
b
 15⟨2,1,0⟩
c
12⟨−1,1,2⟩
d
 13⟨−1,−1,−1⟩
e
 16⟨−1,−1,2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have

B(0)=T(0)×N(0)=13⟨1,1,1⟩×12⟨−1,1,0⟩=16ijk111−110=16[ 1110i−11−10j+11−11k ]=16⟨(0−1),−(0−(−1)),(1−(−1))⟩=16⟨−1,−1,2⟩.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Specific Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(3) & =T(3)\times N(3) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨(-9-16),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨-25,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=3,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(3) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩, \\ N(3) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(3) & =T(3)\times N(3) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨(-9-16),-(0-0),(0-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25}⟨-25,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

T(2)=15⟨0,1,2⟩,N(2)=15⟨0,2,−1⟩.

a
 ⟨0,1,0⟩

 15⟨0,−2,1⟩
c
 ⟨−1,0,0⟩

 15⟨−1,0,2⟩
Submit
Correct

Therefore, we have

question.html:
Question 9
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at the point t=1, given that

T(1)=13⟨2,2,1⟩,N(1)=135⟨−4,5,−2⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
 12⟨1,0,1⟩
b
 13⟨−1,1,1⟩
c
 15⟨3,−4,0⟩
d
 15⟨−1,0,2⟩
e
 13⟨2,1,2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have

B(1)=T(1)×N(1)=13⟨2,2,1⟩×135⟨−4,5,−2⟩=195ijk221−45−2=195[ 215−2i−21−4−2j+22−45k ]=195⟨(−4−5),−(−4−(−4)),(10−(−8))⟩=195⟨−9,0,18⟩=15⟨−1,0,2⟩.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Specific Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Specific Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent and Principal Normal
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =T(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\times N(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨3,5,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨(-15-0),-(-9-16),(0-20)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨-15,25,-20⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨-3,5,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡2$, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨3,5,4⟩, \\ N(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =T(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\times N(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨3,5,4⟩\times \frac{1}{5}⟨4,0,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨(-15-0),-(-9-16),(0-20)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{25\sqrt{2}}⟨-15,25,-20⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}⟨-3,5,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at the point t=ln⁡2, given that

T(ln⁡2)=152⟨3,5,4⟩,N(ln⁡2)=15⟨4,0,−3⟩.

Note that T and N denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

a
12⟨1,0,−1⟩
b
 12⟨2,0,−1⟩
c
 152⟨−3,5,−4⟩
d
 110⟨1,0,3⟩
e
15⟨−2,1,0⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Therefore, we have

B(ln⁡2)=T(ln⁡2)×N(ln⁡2)=152⟨3,5,4⟩×15⟨4,0,−3⟩=1252ijk35440−3=1252[ 540−3i−344−3j+3540k ]=1252⟨(−15−0),−(−9−16),(0−20)⟩=1252⟨−15,25,−20⟩=152⟨−3,5,−4⟩.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf B(t) = \mathbf T(t) \times \mathbf N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $\mathbf N(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $\mathbf{N}(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡4t+16{sin}^{2}⁡4t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡4t+{sin}^{2}⁡4t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{16} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize $\mathbf T'(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩}{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}})} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,2,\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡4t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡4t & 2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t & \operatorname{cos}⁡4t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t & 2 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡4t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡4t-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡4t-{cos}^{2}⁡4t),0-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,1,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The binormal vector is given by

$$

$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡5t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡5t+25{cos}^{2}⁡5t} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-5\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩}{(\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}})}=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡5t,\,-1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡5t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & \operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -1 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡5t-0,-({cos}^{2}⁡5t+{sin}^{2}⁡5t),0-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡5t,\,-1,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=12⟨cos⁡5t,−1,sin⁡5t⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 ⟨sin⁡5t,0,−cos⁡5t⟩
b
 12⟨−cos⁡5t,−1,−sin⁡5t⟩
c
 12⟨cos⁡5t,−2,sin⁡5t⟩
d
 12⟨cos⁡5t,−sin⁡5t,−1⟩
e
 12⟨−cos⁡5t,−2,−sin⁡5t⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=12⟨ddt(cos⁡5t),ddt(−1),ddt(sin⁡5t)⟩=12⟨−5sin⁡5t,0,5cos⁡5t⟩‖T′(t)‖=12(−5sin⁡5t)2+(0)2+(5cos⁡5t)2=1225sin2⁡5t+25cos2⁡5t=52

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=12⟨−5sin⁡5t,0,5cos⁡5t⟩(52)=⟨−sin⁡5t,0,cos⁡5t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=12⟨cos⁡5t,−1,sin⁡5t⟩×⟨−sin⁡5t,0,cos⁡5t⟩=12ijkcos⁡5t−1sin⁡5t−sin⁡5t0cos⁡5t=12[ −1sin⁡5t0cos⁡5ti−cos⁡5tsin⁡5t−sin⁡5tcos⁡5tj+cos⁡5t−1−sin⁡5t0k ]=12⟨−cos⁡5t−0,−(cos2⁡5t+sin2⁡5t),0−sin⁡5t⟩=12⟨−cos⁡5t,−1,−sin⁡5t⟩
