Question 12
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=13⟨22,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 12⟨2,2sin⁡t,−2cos⁡t⟩
b
 12⟨1,sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
c
 13⟨1,2sin⁡t,−2cos⁡t⟩
d
 13⟨1,−2sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
e
13⟨1,22sin⁡t,−22cos⁡t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=13⟨ddt(22),ddt(−sin⁡t),ddt(cos⁡t)⟩=13⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩‖T′(t)‖=13(0)2+(−cos⁡t)2+(−sin⁡t)2=13cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t=13

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=13⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩(13)=⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=13⟨22,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩×⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩=13ijk22−sin⁡tcos⁡t0−cos⁡t−sin⁡t=13[ −sin⁡tcos⁡t−cos⁡t−sin⁡ti−22cos⁡t0−sin⁡tj+22−sin⁡t0−cos⁡tk ]=13⟨(sin2⁡t−(−cos2⁡t)),−(−22sin⁡t−0),(−22cos⁡t−0)⟩=13⟨1,22sin⁡t,−22cos⁡t⟩

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
last_observation.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨({sin}^{2}⁡t-(-{cos}^{2}⁡t)),-(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-0),(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.

Question 12
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=13⟨22,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 12⟨2,2sin⁡t,−2cos⁡t⟩
b
 12⟨1,sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩
c
 13⟨1,2sin⁡t,−2cos⁡t⟩
d
 13⟨1,−2sin⁡t,2cos⁡t⟩
e
13⟨1,22sin⁡t,−22cos⁡t⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=13⟨ddt(22),ddt(−sin⁡t),ddt(cos⁡t)⟩=13⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩‖T′(t)‖=13(0)2+(−cos⁡t)2+(−sin⁡t)2=13cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t=13

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=13⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩(13)=⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=13⟨22,−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩×⟨0,−cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩=13ijk22−sin⁡tcos⁡t0−cos⁡t−sin⁡t=13[ −sin⁡tcos⁡t−cos⁡t−sin⁡ti−22cos⁡t0−sin⁡tj+22−sin⁡t0−cos⁡tk ]=13⟨(sin2⁡t−(−cos2⁡t)),−(−22sin⁡t−0),(−22cos⁡t−0)⟩=13⟨1,22sin⁡t,−22cos⁡t⟩

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
feedback.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2\sqrt{2},-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨({sin}^{2}⁡t-(-{cos}^{2}⁡t)),-(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-0),(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-0)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{5{e}^{2t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(2{e}^{t})^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-5{e}^{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}+25{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-5{e}^{2t}-1,-(-10{e}^{2t}-2),2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,2(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2,0⟩\end{aligned}

Question 13
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨−1,0,2⟩
b
 16⟨−1,−2,1⟩
c
 16⟨2,1,−1⟩
d
 15⟨−1,2,0⟩
e
 12⟨−1,−1,0⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=⟨ddt(2et5e2t+1),ddt(et5e2t+1),ddt(15e2t+1)⟩=⟨2et(5e2t+1)3/2,et(5e2t+1)3/2,−5e2t(5e2t+1)3/2⟩=1(5e2t+1)3/2⟨2et,et,−5e2t⟩‖T′(t)‖=1(5e2t+1)3/2(2et)2+(et)2+(−5e2t)2=1(5e2t+1)3/24e2t+e2t+25e4t=5et(5e2t+1)3/21+5e2t=5et5e2t+1

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=1(5e2t+1)3/2⟨2et,et,−5e2t⟩(5et5e2t+1)=155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩×155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩=15(5e2t+1)ijk2etet121−5et=15(5e2t+1)[ et11−5eti−2et12−5etj+2etet21k ]=15(5e2t+1)⟨−5e2t−1,−(−10e2t−2),2et−2et⟩=15(5e2t+1)⟨−(5e2t+1),2(5e2t+1),0⟩=15⟨−1,2,0⟩

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
last_observation.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{5{e}^{2t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(2{e}^{t})^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-5{e}^{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}+25{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-5{e}^{2t}-1,-(-10{e}^{2t}-2),2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,2(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.

question.html:
Question 13
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨−1,0,2⟩
b
 16⟨−1,−2,1⟩
c
 16⟨2,1,−1⟩
d
 15⟨−1,2,0⟩
e
 12⟨−1,−1,0⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=⟨ddt(2et5e2t+1),ddt(et5e2t+1),ddt(15e2t+1)⟩=⟨2et(5e2t+1)3/2,et(5e2t+1)3/2,−5e2t(5e2t+1)3/2⟩=1(5e2t+1)3/2⟨2et,et,−5e2t⟩‖T′(t)‖=1(5e2t+1)3/2(2et)2+(et)2+(−5e2t)2=1(5e2t+1)3/24e2t+e2t+25e4t=5et(5e2t+1)3/21+5e2t=5et5e2t+1

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=1(5e2t+1)3/2⟨2et,et,−5e2t⟩(5et5e2t+1)=155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩×155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩=15(5e2t+1)ijk2etet121−5et=15(5e2t+1)[ et11−5eti−2et12−5etj+2etet21k ]=15(5e2t+1)⟨−5e2t−1,−(−10e2t−2),2et−2et⟩=15(5e2t+1)⟨−(5e2t+1),2(5e2t+1),0⟩=15⟨−1,2,0⟩
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent

solution.reasoning: Let u=e^t>0 and D=5u²+1. Differentiating gives T′=u⟨2,1,−5u⟩/D^(3/2), with magnitude √5u/D. Hence N=⟨2,1,−5u⟩/√(5D). The cross product B=T×N=⟨−D,2D,0⟩/(√5D)=⟨−1,2,0⟩/√5, option d. feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
feedback.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{5{e}^{2t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(2{e}^{t})^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}+{(-5{e}^{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t}+25{e}^{4t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\sqrt{1+5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{(5{e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t},\,-5{e}^{2t}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{5}{e}^{t}}{5{e}^{2t}+1})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2{e}^{t},{e}^{t},1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5{e}^{2t}+1}}⟨2,\,1,\,-5{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 1 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 1 \\ 2 & -5{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & {e}^{t} \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-5{e}^{2t}-1,-(-10{e}^{2t}-2),2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(5{e}^{2t}+1)}⟨-(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,2(5{e}^{2t}+1),\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨-1,2,0⟩\end{aligned}

T(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨−1,0,2⟩

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=1(5e2t+1)3/2⟨2et,et,−5e2t⟩(5et5e2t+1)=155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=15e2t+1⟨2et,et,1⟩×155e2t+1⟨2,1,−5et⟩=15(5e2t+1)ijk2etet121−5et=15(5e2t+1)[ et11−5eti−2et12−5etj+2etet21k ]=15(5e2t+1)⟨−5e2t−1,−(−10e2t−2),2et−2et⟩=15(5e2t+1)⟨−(5e2t+1),2(5e2t+1),0⟩=15⟨−1,2,0⟩

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)-{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)),0-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),\,1,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=13⟨sin⁡(t+1),22,cos⁡(t+1)⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 12⟨−sin⁡(t+1),1,−cos⁡(t+1)⟩
b
 12⟨3sin⁡(t+1),3cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
c
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),22cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
d
 12⟨−3sin⁡(t+1),1,3cos⁡(t+1)⟩
e
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),1,−22cos⁡(t+1)⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows: T′(t)=13⟨ddt(sin⁡(t+1)),ddt(22),ddt(cos⁡(t+1))⟩=13⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩‖T′(t)‖=13(cos⁡(t+1))2+(0)2+(−sin⁡(t+1))2=13cos2⁡(t+1)+sin2⁡(t+1)=13

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=13⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩(13)=⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
last_observation.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)-{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)),0-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),\,1,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:

$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=13⟨sin⁡(t+1),22,cos⁡(t+1)⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 12⟨−sin⁡(t+1),1,−cos⁡(t+1)⟩
b
 12⟨3sin⁡(t+1),3cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
c
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),22cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
d
 12⟨−3sin⁡(t+1),1,3cos⁡(t+1)⟩
e
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),1,−22cos⁡(t+1)⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows: T′(t)=13⟨ddt(sin⁡(t+1)),ddt(22),ddt(cos⁡(t+1))⟩=13⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩‖T′(t)‖=13(cos⁡(t+1))2+(0)2+(−sin⁡(t+1))2=13cos2⁡(t+1)+sin2⁡(t+1)=13

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=13⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩(13)=⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=13⟨sin⁡(t+1),22,cos⁡(t+1)⟩×⟨cos⁡(t+1),0,−sin⁡(t+1)⟩=13ijksin⁡(t+1)22cos⁡(t+1)cos⁡(t+1)0−sin⁡(t+1)=13[ 22cos⁡(t+1)0−sin⁡(t+1)i−sin⁡(t+1)cos⁡(t+1)cos⁡(t+1)−sin⁡(t+1)j+sin⁡(t+1)22cos⁡(t+1)0k ]=13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1)−0,−(−sin2⁡(t+1)−cos2⁡(t+1)),0−22cos⁡(t+1)⟩=13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),1,−22cos⁡(t+1)⟩

solution.reasoning: T′(t)=(1/3)⟨cos(t+1),0,−sin(t+1)⟩ has magnitude 1/3, so N(t)=⟨cos(t+1),0,−sin(t+1)⟩. Thus B=T×N=(1/3)⟨−2√2 sin(t+1),sin²(t+1)+cos²(t+1),−2√2 cos(t+1)⟩, which simplifies to option e. feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
feedback.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})}=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),2\sqrt{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\times ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1),\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1) & 2\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1)-0,-(-{sin}^{2}⁡(t+1)-{cos}^{2}⁡(t+1)),0-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+1),\,1,\,-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=13⟨sin⁡(t+1),22,cos⁡(t+1)⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 12⟨−sin⁡(t+1),1,−cos⁡(t+1)⟩
b
 12⟨3sin⁡(t+1),3cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
c
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),22cos⁡(t+1),−1⟩
d
 12⟨−3sin⁡(t+1),1,3cos⁡(t+1)⟩
e
 13⟨−22sin⁡(t+1),1,−22cos⁡(t+1)⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
question.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,\frac{4t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(5)^{2}+(-4t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{25+16{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{20{t}^{2}+25} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩}{(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,2,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2t & -1 \\ 5 & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 5 & -4t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨4t-4t,-(4{t}^{2}+5),-8{t}^{2}-10⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨0,\,-(4{t}^{2}+5),\,-2(4{t}^{2}+5)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨1,0,−2⟩
b
 15⟨0,−2,1⟩
c
⟨0,−1,0⟩
d
 13⟨0,−1,2⟩
e
 15⟨0,−1,−2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=⟨ddt(2t4t2+5),ddt(24t2+5),ddt(−14t2+5)⟩=⟨10(4t2+5)3/2,−8t(4t2+5)3/2,4t(4t2+5)3/2⟩=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2(5)2+(−4t)2+(2t)2=2(4t2+5)3/225+16t2+4t2=2(4t2+5)3/220t2+25=25(4t2+5)3/24t2+5=254t2+5

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩(254t2+5)=154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩×154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩=15(4t2+5)ijk2t2−15−4t2t=15(4t2+5)[ 2−1−4t2ti−2t−152tj+2t25−4tk ]=15(4t2+5)⟨4t−4t,−(4t2+5),−8t2−10⟩=15(4t2+5)⟨0,−(4t2+5),−2(4t2+5)⟩=15⟨0,−1,−2⟩

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent
last_observation.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,\frac{4t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(5)^{2}+(-4t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{25+16{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{20{t}^{2}+25} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩}{(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,2,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2t & -1 \\ 5 & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 5 & -4t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨4t-4t,-(4{t}^{2}+5),-8{t}^{2}-10⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨0,\,-(4{t}^{2}+5),\,-2(4{t}^{2}+5)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.

question.html:
Question 15
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨1,0,−2⟩
b
 15⟨0,−2,1⟩
c
⟨0,−1,0⟩
d
 13⟨0,−1,2⟩
e
 15⟨0,−1,−2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=⟨ddt(2t4t2+5),ddt(24t2+5),ddt(−14t2+5)⟩=⟨10(4t2+5)3/2,−8t(4t2+5)3/2,4t(4t2+5)3/2⟩=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2(5)2+(−4t)2+(2t)2=2(4t2+5)3/225+16t2+4t2=2(4t2+5)3/220t2+25=25(4t2+5)3/24t2+5=254t2+5

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩(254t2+5)=154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩×154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩=15(4t2+5)ijk2t2−15−4t2t=15(4t2+5)[ 2−1−4t2ti−2t−152tj+2t25−4tk ]=15(4t2+5)⟨4t−4t,−(4t2+5),−8t2−10⟩=15(4t2+5)⟨0,−(4t2+5),−2(4t2+5)⟩=15⟨0,−1,−2⟩
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the General Binormal Vector to a Curve Given the Unit Tangent

solution.reasoning: Let D=4t²+5. Differentiating gives T′=⟨10,−8t,4t⟩/D^(3/2), with magnitude 2√5/D. Since T×T′=⟨0,−2,−4⟩/D, the binormal B=(T×T′)/‖T′‖=⟨0,−1,−2⟩/√5, option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem:
Find the binormal vector to the curve $r(t)$ at an arbitrary point, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ denotes the unit tangent vector.
feedback.worked_solution:
The binormal vector is given by

$$
B(t)=T(t)\times N(t),
$$

where the principal normal vector $N(t)$ is given by

$$
N(t)=\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,-\frac{8t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}},\,\frac{4t}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{(5)^{2}+(-4t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{25+16{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{20{t}^{2}+25} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{2}{(4{t}^{2}+5)^{3/2}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩}{(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4{t}^{2}+5})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =T(t)\times N(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨2t,2,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+5}}⟨5,\,-4t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4t & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}2t & -1 \\ 5 & 2t\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 5 & -4t\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨4t-4t,-(4{t}^{2}+5),-8{t}^{2}-10⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}(4{t}^{2}+5)}⟨0,\,-(4{t}^{2}+5),\,-2(4{t}^{2}+5)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

Find the binormal vector to the curve r(t) at an arbitrary point, given that

T(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩.

Note that T denotes the unit tangent vector.

a
 15⟨1,0,−2⟩
b
 15⟨0,−2,1⟩
c
⟨0,−1,0⟩
d
 13⟨0,−1,2⟩
e
 15⟨0,−1,−2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The binormal vector is given by B(t)=T(t)×N(t),

where the principal normal vector N(t) is given by

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖.

First, we find the principal normal N(t). To do this, we calculate T′(t) and its magnitude as follows:

T′(t)=⟨ddt(2t4t2+5),ddt(24t2+5),ddt(−14t2+5)⟩=⟨10(4t2+5)3/2,−8t(4t2+5)3/2,4t(4t2+5)3/2⟩=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2(5)2+(−4t)2+(2t)2=2(4t2+5)3/225+16t2+4t2=2(4t2+5)3/220t2+25=25(4t2+5)3/24t2+5=254t2+5

Now, we normalize T′(t) and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

N(t)=T′(t)‖T′(t)‖=2(4t2+5)3/2⟨5,−4t,2t⟩(254t2+5)=154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩

Finally, we calculate the binormal vector, as follows: B(t)=T(t)×N(t)=14t2+5⟨2t,2,−1⟩×154t2+5⟨5,−4t,2t⟩=15(4t2+5)ijk2t2−15−4t2t=15(4t2+5)[ 2−1−4t2ti−2t−152tj+2t25−4tk ]=15(4t2+5)⟨4t−4t,−(4t2+5),−8t2−10⟩=15(4t2+5)⟨0,−(4t2+5),−2(4t2+5)⟩=15⟨0,−1,−2⟩

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What number is $125%$ greater than $64?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find a number $125%$ *greater than* $64,$ we apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+125%=225%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
225%=\frac{225}{100}=2.25
$$

So, to find a number that is $125%$ greater than $64,$ we multiply $64$ by $2.25:$

$$
2.25\cdot 64=144
$$

Therefore, the number that is $125%$ greater than $64$ is $144.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: A sandwich costs $$12$ before tax. If a $9.5%$ sales tax is applied, what is the total price after tax?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the total price after tax, we apply a $9.5%$ increase to the original cost.

Increasing by $9.5%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+9.5%=109.5%=1.095
$$

Now, we multiply the original price by $1.095:$

$$
12\times 1.095=13.14.
$$

So, the total price after tax is $$13.14.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: A country welcomed $3,\,500,\,000$ tourists in $2018.$  Travel authorities predict that this number will increase by $45%$ by the year $2028.$ Which of the following is closest to the projected number of tourists in $2028?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the projected number of tourists in $2028,$ we apply a $45%$ increase to the $2018$ figure.

Increasing by $45%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+45%=145%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
145%=\frac{145}{100}=1.45
$$

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by $1.45:$

$$
3,\,500,\,000\times 1.45=5,\,075,\,000
$$

Therefore, the projected number of tourists in $2028$ is $5,\,075,\,000.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
A factory produced $900$ boxes of cereal last year. This year, production is $300%$ greater than last year. How many boxes of cereal did the factory produce this year?

The factory produced
{{field-1}}
boxes of cereal this year.
questions.worked_solution:
To find this year's cereal production, we apply a $300%$ increase to last year's figure.

Increasing by $300%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+300%=400%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
400%=\frac{400}{100}=4
$$

Now, we multiply the original amount by $4:$

$$
900\times 4=3,600
$$

So, the factory produced $3600$ boxes of cereal this year.

A country welcomed 3,500,000 tourists in 2018. Travel authorities predict that this number will increase by 45% by the year 2028. Which of the following is closest to the projected number of tourists in 2028?

a
5,100,000
b
5,075,000
c
5,025,000
d
5,050,000
e
5,000,000
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the projected number of tourists in 2028, we apply a 45% increase to the 2018 figure.

Increasing by 45% means that we must apply a new percentage of

100%+45%=145%.

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

145%=145100=1.45

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by 1.45:

3,500,000×1.45=5,075,000

Therefore, the projected number of tourists in 2028 is 5,075,000.

question.problem: What number is $125%$ greater than $64?$
question.worked_solution:
To find a number $125%$ *greater than* $64,$ we apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+125%=225%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
225%=\frac{225}{100}=2.25
$$

So, to find a number that is $125%$ greater than $64,$ we multiply $64$ by $2.25:$

$$
2.25\cdot 64=144
$$

Therefore, the number that is $125%$ greater than $64$ is $144.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: A sandwich costs $$12$ before tax. If a $9.5%$ sales tax is applied, what is the total price after tax?
question.worked_solution:
To find the total price after tax, we apply a $9.5%$ increase to the original cost.

Increasing by $9.5%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+9.5%=109.5%=1.095
$$

Now, we multiply the original price by $1.095:$

$$
12\times 1.095=13.14.
$$

Question 3
?

A sandwich costs $12 before tax. If a 9.5% sales tax is applied, what is the total price after tax?

a
$13.14
b
$12.95
c
$13.50
d
$14.00
e
$12.75
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the total price after tax, we apply a 9.5% increase to the original cost.

Increasing by 9.5% means that we must apply a new percentage of

100%+9.5%=109.5%=1.095

Now, we multiply the original price by 1.095:

12×1.095=13.14.

So, the total price after tax is $13.14.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: A country welcomed $3,\,500,\,000$ tourists in $2018.$  Travel authorities predict that this number will increase by $45%$ by the year $2028.$ Which of the following is closest to the projected number of tourists in $2028?$
question.worked_solution:
To find the projected number of tourists in $2028,$ we apply a $45%$ increase to the $2018$ figure.

Increasing by $45%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+45%=145%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
145%=\frac{145}{100}=1.45
$$

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by $1.45:$

$$
3,\,500,\,000\times 1.45=5,\,075,\,000
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A country welcomed 3,500,000 tourists in 2018. Travel authorities predict that this number will increase by 45% by the year 2028. Which of the following is closest to the projected number of tourists in 2028?

a
5,100,000
b
5,075,000
c
5,025,000
d
5,050,000
e
5,000,000
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the projected number of tourists in 2028, we apply a 45% increase to the 2018 figure.

Increasing by 45% means that we must apply a new percentage of

100%+45%=145%.

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

145%=145100=1.45

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by 1.45:

3,500,000×1.45=5,075,000

Therefore, the projected number of tourists in 2028 is 5,075,000.

question.html:
Question 4
?

A country welcomed 3,500,000 tourists in 2018. Travel authorities predict that this number will increase by 45% by the year 2028. Which of the following is closest to the projected number of tourists in 2028?

a
5,100,000
b
5,075,000
c
5,025,000
d
5,050,000
e
5,000,000
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the projected number of tourists in 2028, we apply a 45% increase to the 2018 figure.

Increasing by 45% means that we must apply a new percentage of

100%+45%=145%.

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

145%=145100=1.45

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by 1.45:

3,500,000×1.45=5,075,000

Therefore, the projected number of tourists in 2028 is 5,075,000.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
A wildlife reserve is monitoring the population of a newly introduced species of deer. The habitat can sustain a maximum population of $850$ deer, but the herd is still below this limit. Since biologists began tracking the growth, the population reached $490$ deer on month $4$ and $600$ deer on month $12.$ On what month will the population reach $800$ deer? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the population of deer, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in months.*
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=850$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(850-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{850-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{850-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|850-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $850-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}850-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 850-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 850-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =850-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population reached $490$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(4)=490,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =490 \\ 850-K{e}^{-4k} & =490 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =360.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $12,$ the population was $600$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(12)=600,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =600 \\ 850-K{e}^{-12k} & =600 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-12k}} & =\frac{360}{250} \\ {e}^{8k} & =\frac{36}{25} \\ 8k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} & =360 \\ K & =360{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} \\ K & =360\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}} \\ K & =360\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ K & =432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=850-432{e}^{-(t/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)}
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $800$ deer. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =800 \\ 850-432{e}^{-km} & =800 \\ 50 & =432{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{50}{432} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the population will be $500$ deer on month

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216})}{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})}=47.309…≈47,
$$

rounded to the nearest month.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A national park is monitoring the number of people who have downloaded a new park app. The system can support a maximum of $800$ users, but the total is still below this limit. Since the park began tracking downloads, the number of users reached $620$ on day $3$ and $720$ on day $9.$ On what day will the number of users reach $760?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the number of users, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in days.*
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the number of app users $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of users the system can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=800$ users, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(800-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{800-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{800-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|800-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $800-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}800-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 800-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 800-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =800-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $3,$ the number of users was $620.$ So, applying the condition $P(3)=620,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3) & =620 \\ 800-K{e}^{-3k} & =620 \\ K{e}^{-3k} & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $9,$ the number of users was $720.$ So, applying the condition $P(9)=720,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(9) & =720 \\ 800-K{e}^{-9k} & =720 \\ K{e}^{-9k} & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-3k}}{K{e}^{-9k}} & =\frac{180}{80} \\ {e}^{6k} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ 6k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-3\cdot (1/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)} & =180 \\ K & =180{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)} \\ K & =180\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ K & =180\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=800-270{e}^{-(t/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)}.
$$

Finally, let $d$  be the day when the app reaches $760$ users. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(d) & =760 \\ 800-270{e}^{-kd} & =760 \\ 40 & =270{e}^{-kd} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =\frac{40}{270} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =\frac{4}{27} \\ -kd & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27}) \\ d & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the number of users will be $760$ on day

$$
d=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27})}{\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4})}=14.1285…≈14,
$$

rounded to the nearest day.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A mountain valley is monitoring the population of a reintroduced elk herd. The valley can sustain a maximum population of $600$ elk, but the herd is still below this limit. Since ecologists began tracking the growth, the population reached $536$ elk on month $4$ and $573$ elk on month $10.$ On what month will the population reach $590$ elk? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the population of elk, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in months.*
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum population the valley can sustain, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=600$ elk, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(600-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{600-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{600-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|600-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $600-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}600-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 600-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 600-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =600-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population was $536$ elk. So, applying the condition $P(4)=536,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =536 \\ 600-K{e}^{-4k} & =536 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =64.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $10,$ the population was $573$ elk. So, applying the condition $P(10)=573,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10) & =573 \\ 600-K{e}^{-10k} & =573 \\ K{e}^{-10k} & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-10k}} & =\frac{64}{27} \\ {e}^{6k} & =\frac{64}{27} \\ 6k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{64}{27}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{64}{27})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(64/27)} & =64 \\ K & =64{e}^{(4/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(64/27)} \\ K & =64{e}^{(2/3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(64/27)} \\ K & =64{(\frac{64}{27})}^{2/3} \\ K & =\frac{1\,024}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=600-\frac{1\,024}{9}{e}^{-(t/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(64/27)}.
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $590$ elk. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =590 \\ 600-\frac{1\,024}{9}{e}^{-km} & =590 \\ 10 & =\frac{1\,024}{9}{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{90}{1\,024} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{45}{512} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{45}{512}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{45}{512}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the population will be $590$ elk on month

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{45}{512})}{\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{64}{27})}=16.905…≈17,
$$

rounded to the nearest day.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhibited Growth Model
questions.raw_html:
3.Solving an Inhibited Growth Model?

A mountain valley is monitoring the population of a reintroduced elk herd. The valley can sustain a maximum population of 600 elk, but the herd is still below this limit. Since ecologists began tracking the growth, the population reached 536 elk on month 4 and 573 elk on month 10. On what month will the population reach 590 elk? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

Hint: You may assume that the population of elk, P(t), increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t is the time, in months.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: A hospital administrator observed that the growth of the number of occupied beds in a hospital is directly proportional to the difference between the hospital’s maximum bed capacity and the current number of occupied beds. Let $H(t)$ be the number of occupied beds, measured in beds, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in years. If the maximum number of beds the hospital can support is $75$ beds, which differential equation could be used to model the number of occupied beds in the hospital? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the number of occupied beds $H(t)$ in the hospital changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum number of beds the hospital can support and the current number of occupied beds. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=k(a-H),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of beds the hospital can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=75\text{ beds},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=k(75-H).
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: A data center initially contains $320$ computers. The number of computers in the data center $C(t)$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t\ge 0$ is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the data center is $1000$ computers, which differential equation could be used to model the number of computers? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the number of computers in the data center obeys an inhibited growth model, the rate at which the number of computers changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the number of computers in the data center. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=k(a-C),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity of the data center, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=1000$ computers, and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=k(1000-C).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Modeling Inhibited Growth
questions.raw_html:
5.Modeling Inhibited Growth?

A data center initially contains 320 computers. The number of computers in the data center C(t) increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t≥0 is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the data center is 1000 computers, which differential equation could be used to model the number of computers? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

E

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=850$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(850-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{850-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{850-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|850-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $850-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}850-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 850-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 850-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =850-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population reached $490$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(4)=490,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =490 \\ 850-K{e}^{-4k} & =490 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =360.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $12,$ the population was $600$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(12)=600,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =600 \\ 850-K{e}^{-12k} & =600 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-12k}} & =\frac{360}{250} \\ {e}^{8k} & =\frac{36}{25} \\ 8k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} & =360 \\ K & =360{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} \\ K & =360\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}} \\ K & =360\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ K & =432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=850-432{e}^{-(t/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)}
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $800$ deer. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =800 \\ 850-432{e}^{-km} & =800 \\ 50 & =432{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{50}{432} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the population will be $500$ deer on month

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216})}{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})}=47.309…≈47,
$$

rounded to the nearest month.

question.problem:
A wildlife reserve is monitoring the population of a newly introduced species of deer. The habitat can sustain a maximum population of $850$ deer, but the herd is still below this limit. Question 1
?

A wildlife reserve is monitoring the population of a newly introduced species of deer. The habitat can sustain a maximum population of 850 deer, but the herd is still below this limit. Since biologists began tracking the growth, the population reached 490 deer on month 4 and 600 deer on month 12. On what month will the population reach 800 deer? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

Hint: You may assume that the population of deer, P(t), increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t is the time, in months.

a
56th month
b
60th month
c
40th month
d
47th month
e
48th month
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The rate at which the population P(t) changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation dPdt=k(a−P), where a is the maximum production of the farm, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=850 deer, and we have dPdt=k(850−P).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

dP850−P=kdt∫dP850−P=∫kdt−ln⁡|850−P|=kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have 850−P>0 for all t≥0. Next, we solve for P(t), as follows:

850−P=e−kt−C850−P=e−Ce−kt850−P=Ke−ktP=850−Ke−kt

Note that K=e−C is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month 4, the population reached 490 deer. So, applying the condition P(4)=490, we have P(4)=490850−Ke−4k=490Ke−4k=360.

We're also told that, on month 12, the population was 600 deer. So, applying the condition P(12)=600, we get P(12)=600850−Ke−12k=600Ke−12k=250.

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for k:

Ke−4kKe−12k=360250e8k=36258k=ln⁡(3625)k=18ln⁡(3625)

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for K:

Ke−4⋅(1/8)ln⁡(36/25)=360K=360e(1/2)ln⁡(36/25)K=3603625K=360⋅65K=432

Therefore, we have the following expression for P(t):

P(t)=850−432e−(t/8)ln⁡(36/25)

Finally, let m be the month when the population reaches 800 deer. Then, we have

P(m)=800850−432e−km=80050=432e−kme−km=50432−km=ln⁡(25216)m=−1kln⁡(25216).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the population will be 500 deer on month m=−ln⁡(25216)18ln⁡(3625)=47.309…≈47,

rounded to the nearest month.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The rate at which the number of app users $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of users the system can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=800$ users, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(800-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{800-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{800-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|800-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $800-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}800-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 800-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 800-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =800-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $3,$ the number of users was $620.$ So, applying the condition $P(3)=620,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3) & =620 \\ 800-K{e}^{-3k} & =620 \\ K{e}^{-3k} & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $9,$ the number of users was $720.$ So, applying the condition $P(9)=720,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(9) & =720 \\ 800-K{e}^{-9k} & =720 \\ K{e}^{-9k} & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-3k}}{K{e}^{-9k}} & =\frac{180}{80} \\ {e}^{6k} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ 6k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-3\cdot (1/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)} & =180 \\ K & =180{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)} \\ K & =180\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ K & =180\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\ K & =270\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=800-270{e}^{-(t/6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9/4)}.
$$

Finally, let $d$  be the day when the app reaches $760$ users. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(d) & =760 \\ 800-270{e}^{-kd} & =760 \\ 40 & =270{e}^{-kd} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =\frac{40}{270} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =\frac{4}{27} \\ -kd & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27}) \\ d & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the number of users will be $760$ on day

$$
d=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{27})}{\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{9}{4})}=14.1285…≈14,
$$

rounded to the nearest day.

question.html:
Question 3
?

A mountain valley is monitoring the population of a reintroduced elk herd. The valley can sustain a maximum population of 600 elk, but the herd is still below this limit. Since ecologists began tracking the growth, the population reached 536 elk on month 4 and 573 elk on month 10. On what month will the population reach 590 elk? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

Hint: You may assume that the population of elk, P(t), increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t is the time, in months.

a
20th month
b
17th month
c
25th month
d
14th month
e
22th month
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The rate at which the population P(t) changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation dPdt=k(a−P), where a is the maximum population the valley can sustain, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=600 elk, and we have dPdt=k(600−P).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables: dP600−P=kdt∫dP600−P=∫kdt−ln⁡|600−P|=kt+C

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have 600−P>0 for all t≥0. Next, we solve for P(t), as follows: 600−P=e−kt−C600−P=e−Ce−kt600−P=Ke−ktP=600−Ke−kt

Note that K=e−C is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month 4, the population was 536 elk. So, applying the condition P(4)=536, we have P(4)=536600−Ke−4k=536Ke−4k=64.

We're also told that, on month 10, the population was 573 elk. So, applying the condition P(10)=573, we get P(10)=573600−Ke−10k=573Ke−10k=27.

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for k: Ke−4kKe−10k=6427e6k=64276k=ln⁡(6427)k=16ln⁡(6427)

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for K: Ke−4⋅(1/6)ln⁡(64/27)=64K=64e(4/6)ln⁡(64/27)K=64e(2/3)ln⁡(64/27)K=64(6427)2/3K=10249

Therefore, we have the following expression for P(t): P(t)=600−10249e−(t/6)ln⁡(64/27).

Finally, let m be the month when the population reaches 590 elk. Then, we have

P(m)=590600−10249e−km=59010=10249e−kme−km=901024e−km=45512−km=ln⁡(45512)m=−1kln⁡(45512).

Substituting in our value for k, we conclude that the population will be 590 elk on month m=−ln⁡(45512)16ln⁡(6427)=16.905…≈17, rounded to the nearest day.

Question 5
?

A data center initially contains 320 computers. The number of computers in the data center C(t) increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where t≥0 is the time in months. If the maximum capacity of the data center is 1000 computers, which differential equation could be used to model the number of computers? Assume that k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

a
dCdt=k(500−C)
b
dCdt=k(1000−C)
c
dCdt=k(800−C)
d
dCdt=k(1500−C)
e
dCdt=k(320−C)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the number of computers in the data center obeys an inhibited growth model, the rate at which the number of computers changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the number of computers in the data center. Therefore, we have the differential equation dCdt=k(a−C),

where a is the maximum capacity of the data center, and k>0 is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, a=1000 computers, and we have

dCdt=k(1000−C).

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
A wildlife reserve is monitoring the population of a newly introduced species of deer. The habitat can sustain a maximum population of $850$ deer, but the herd is still below this limit. Since biologists began tracking the growth, the population reached $490$ deer on month $4$ and $600$ deer on month $12.$ On what month will the population reach $800$ deer? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the population of deer, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in months.*
question.worked_solution:
The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=850$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(850-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{850-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{850-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|850-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $850-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}850-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 850-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 850-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =850-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population reached $490$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(4)=490,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =490 \\ 850-K{e}^{-4k} & =490 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =360.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $12,$ the population was $600$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(12)=600,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =600 \\ 850-K{e}^{-12k} & =600 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-12k}} & =\frac{360}{250} \\ {e}^{8k} & =\frac{36}{25} \\ 8k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} & =360 \\ K & =360{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} \\ K & =360\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}} \\ K & =360\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ K & =432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=850-432{e}^{-(t/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)}
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $800$ deer. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =800 \\ 850-432{e}^{-km} & =800 \\ 50 & =432{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{50}{432} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the population will be $500$ deer on month

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216})}{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})}=47.309…≈47,
$$

rounded to the nearest month.

The rate at which the population $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=850$ deer, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(850-P).

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{850-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{850-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|850-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $850-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}850-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ 850-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ 850-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =850-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on month $4,$ the population reached $490$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(4)=490,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4) & =490 \\ 850-K{e}^{-4k} & =490 \\ K{e}^{-4k} & =360.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on month $12,$ the population was $600$ deer. So, applying the condition $P(12)=600,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(12) & =600 \\ 850-K{e}^{-12k} & =600 \\ K{e}^{-12k} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-4k}}{K{e}^{-12k}} & =\frac{360}{250} \\ {e}^{8k} & =\frac{36}{25} \\ 8k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25}) \\ k & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-4\cdot (1/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} & =360 \\ K & =360{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)} \\ K & =360\sqrt{\frac{36}{25}} \\ K & =360\cdot \frac{6}{5} \\ K & =432\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=850-432{e}^{-(t/8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(36/25)}
$$

Finally, let $m$ be the month when the population reaches $800$ deer. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(m) & =800 \\ 850-432{e}^{-km} & =800 \\ 50 & =432{e}^{-km} \\ {e}^{-km} & =\frac{50}{432} \\ -km & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}) \\ m & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
m=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{25}{216})}{\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{36}{25})}=47.309…≈47,
$$

rounded to the nearest month.
