observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 16\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$

\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 5-5\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[1−1−3545][2−1]=[3−2]

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 2-4\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x={c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 10-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x={c}_{1}+4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

PB→C=[23610]

a

b
[22]
c
[−11]

[11]
Submit
Incorrect

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[23610]−1=12⋅10−6⋅3[10−3−62]=[5−32−31]

Notice that since x=c1+4c2, we obtain [x]C=[14].

Now, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[5−32−31][14]=[−11]

Question 1
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B={b1,b2} to C={c1,c2} is given below. Find [x]B given that x=c1+4c2.

PB→C=[23610]

a
[5−5]
b
[22]
c
[−11]
d
[−22]
e
[11]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[23610]−1=12⋅10−6⋅3[10−3−62]=[5−32−31]

Notice that since x=c1+4c2, we obtain [x]C=[14].

Now, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[5−32−31][14]=[−11]

solution.reasoning: Since x=c_1+4c_2, [x]_C=(1,4)^T. The coordinate relation P_{B\to C}[x]_B=[x]_C gives 2u+3v=1 and 6u+10v=4. Subtracting three times the first equation from the second yields v=1, then u=-1. Thus option c is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x={c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 10-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x={c}_{1}+4{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 16\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 2
?

B={[13],[516]},[x]S=[27]

The basis B of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the standard basis S are given above. Find [x]B.

a
[−30]
b
[−31]
c
[−51]
d
[30]
e
[31]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[15316].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[15316]−1=11⋅16−3⋅5[16−5−31]=[16−5−31]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[16−5−31][27]=[−31]

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

B={[13],[516]},[x]S=[27]

The basis B of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the standard basis S are given above. Find [x]B.

a
[−30]
b
[−31]
c
[−51]
d
[30]
e
[31]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[15316].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[15316]−1=11⋅16−3⋅5[16−5−31]=[16−5−31]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[16−5−31][27]=[−31]

solution.reasoning: Write x=u(1,3)^T+v(5,16)^T. Then u+5v=2 and 3u+16v=7. Subtracting three times the first equation from the second gives v=1, hence u=-3. Therefore option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 16\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 3 & 16\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 16-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -5 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\},\,C=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Question 3
?

B={[01],[−61]},C={[32],[01]},[x]B=[6−3].

The bases B and C of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the basis B are given above. Find [x]C.

a
[1−7]
b
[45]
c
[8−9]
d
[−36]
e
[6−9]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[300−62111]R1:=13R1∼[100−22111]R2:=R2+(−2)R2∼[100−20115]

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C is PB→C=[0−215].

Finally, we compute [x]C:

[x]C=PB→C[x]B=[0−215][6−3]=[6−9]

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

B={[01],[−61]},C={[32],[01]},[x]B=[6−3].

The bases B and C of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the basis B are given above. Find [x]C.

a
[1−7]
b
[45]
c
[8−9]
d
[−36]
e
[6−9]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[300−62111]R1:=13R1∼[100−22111]R2:=R2+(−2)R2∼[100−20115]

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C is PB→C=[0−215].

Finally, we compute [x]C:

[x]C=PB→C[x]B=[0−215][6−3]=[6−9]

solution.reasoning: In standard coordinates, x=6(0,1)^T-3(-6,1)^T=(18,3)^T. Writing x=u(3,2)^T+v(0,1)^T gives 3u=18 and 2u+v=3, so u=6 and v=-9. Thus option e is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\},\,C=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

The bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given above. Find $[x]_{C}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 5-5\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 4
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B={b1,b2} to C={c1,c2} is given below. Find [x]B given that x=2c1−c2.

PB→C=[4535]

a
[−32]
b
[−23]
c
[3−2]
d
[32]
e
[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[4535]−1=14⋅5−5⋅3[5−5−34]=[1−1−3545]

Notice that since x=2c1−c2, we obtain

[x]C=[2−1].

Now, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[1−1−3545][2−1]=[3−2]

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 5-5\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B={b1,b2} to C={c1,c2} is given below. Find [x]B given that x=2c1−c2.

PB→C=[4535]

a
[−32]
b
[−23]
c
[3−2]
d
[32]
e
[23]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PC→B[x]C.

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PC→B from C to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→C:

PC→B=PB→C−1=[4535]−1=14⋅5−5⋅3[5−5−34]=[1−1−3545]

Notice that since x=2c1−c2, we obtain

[x]C=[2−1].

Now, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PC→B[x]C=[1−1−3545][2−1]=[3−2]

solution.reasoning: Since x=2c_1-c_2, [x]_C=(2,-1)^T. The relation P_{B\to C}[x]_B=[x]_C gives 4u+5v=2 and 3u+5v=-1. Subtracting yields u=3, then v=-2. Thus option c is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ to $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 5-5\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain 

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 2-4\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

B={[31],[42]},[x]S=[82]

The basis B of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the standard basis S are given above. Find [x]B.

a
[1−4]
b
[4−1]
c
[1−1]
d
[−1−1]
e
[−1−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[3412].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[3412]−1=13⋅2−4⋅1[2−4−13]=[1−2−1232]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[1−2−1232][82]=[4−1]

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 2-4\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

B={[31],[42]},[x]S=[82]

The basis B of R2 and the coordinates of the vector x relative to the standard basis S are given above. Find [x]B.

a
[1−4]
b
[4−1]
c
[1−1]
d
[−1−1]
e
[−1−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

[x]B=PS→B[x]S.

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of B relative to the standard basis S. As a result, we have

PB→S=[3412].

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix PS→B from S to B. To do that, we compute the inverse of PB→S:

PS→B=PB→S−1=[3412]−1=13⋅2−4⋅1[2−4−13]=[1−2−1232]

Finally, we compute [x]B:

[x]B=PS→B[x]S=[1−2−1232][82]=[4−1]

solution.reasoning: Write x=u(3,1)^T+v(4,2)^T. Then 3u+4v=8 and u+2v=2. Subtracting twice the second equation from the first gives u=4, hence v=-1. Indeed, 4(3,1)^T-(4,2)^T=(8,2)^T. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 2-4\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=66$ from a population where $42%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,66.$ Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic $X={\sum }_{i=1}^{66}{X}_{i}.$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p).$ 

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=42%=0.42,\,n=66.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(66,0.42).
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=140$ from a population where $60%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,140.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{140}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Properties of Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables
questions.raw_html:
2.Properties of Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables?

Suppose we have a random sample of size n=140 from a population where 60% of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable Xi be equal to Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise where i=1,…,140. If the statistic X is defined as X=∑i=1140Xi find approximate values of E[X] and Var[X].

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.html:
3.Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions?

Suppose that 60% of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of n=20 children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of right-handed children in the sample?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

questions.knowledge_point: Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions
questions.raw_html:
3.Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions?

Suppose that 60% of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of n=20 children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of right-handed children in the sample?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Suppose that $25%$ of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of $n=25$ high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=25%=0.25,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =25%=0.25, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.25(1-0.25)}{25} \\  & =0.0075.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions
questions.raw_html:
4.Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions?

Suppose that 25% of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of n=25 high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
It is known that  $5%$ of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of $n=15$ researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions
questions.raw_html:
5.Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions?

It is known that 5% of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of n=15 researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to 4 decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

M

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p).$ 

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=42%=0.42,\,n=66.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(66,0.42).
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we have a random sample of size n=140 from a population where 60% of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable Xi be equal to Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise where i=1,…,140. If the statistic X is defined as X=∑i=1140Xi find approximate values of E[X] and Var[X].

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[X]=81,Var[X]=30.5
b
E[X]=84,Var[X]=30.5
c
E[X]=81,Var[X]=33.6
d
E[X]=84,Var[X]=36.2
e
E[X]=84,Var[X]=33.6
Submit

EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise

Now, provided that N≫n, the random variables Xi can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have Xi∼Bernoulli(p)1≤i≤n where p is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable X, defined as X=∑i=1nXi can be approximated as a binomial random variable X≈B(n,p), where E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have p=60%=0.6,n=140.

Therefore, X≈B(140,0.6) and we have the following results for the mean and variance: E[X]=np=140⋅0.6=84Var[X]=np(1−p)=140⋅0.6⋅(1−0.6)=33.6

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Suppose that 60% of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of n=20 children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of right-handed children in the sample?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.024
b
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.012
c
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.012
d
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.024
e
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.018
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=60%=0.6, and n=20. Therefore, E[p^]=60%=0.6,Var[p^]=0.6(1−0.6)20=0.012.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=25%=0.25,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =25%=0.25, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.25(1-0.25)}{25} \\  & =0.0075.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*

Question 4

Suppose that 25% of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of n=25 high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0065
b
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0085
c
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0065
d
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0075
e
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0075

EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=25%=0.25, and n=25. Therefore, E[p^]=25%=0.25,Var[p^]=0.25(1−0.25)25=0.0075.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 5
?

It is known that 5% of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of n=15 researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to 4 decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0032
b
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0064
c
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0032
d
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0049
e
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0064
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=5%=0.05, and n=15. Therefore, E[p^]=5%=0.05,Var[p^]=0.05(1−0.05)15≈0.0032 rounded to 4 decimal places.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=66$ from a population where $42%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,66.$ Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic $X={\sum }_{i=1}^{66}{X}_{i}.$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$

Question 1
?

Suppose we have a random sample of size n=66 from a population where 42% of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable Xi be equal to Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise where i=1,…,66. Find an approximate sampling distribution of the statistic X=∑i=166Xi.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
B(66,0.58)
b
Bernoulli(0.42)
c
B(28,0.42)
d
Bernoulli(0.58)
e
B(66,0.42)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise

Now, provided that N≫n, the random variables Xi can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have Xi∼Bernoulli(p)1≤i≤n where p is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable X, defined as X=∑i=1nXi can be approximated as a binomial random variable X≈B(n,p).

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have p=42%=0.42,n=66. Therefore, X≈B(66,0.42).

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=140$ from a population where $60%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,140.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{140}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Suppose we have a random sample of size n=140 from a population where 60% of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable Xi be equal to Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise where i=1,…,140. If the statistic X is defined as X=∑i=1140Xi find approximate values of E[X] and Var[X].

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[X]=81,Var[X]=30.5
b
E[X]=84,Var[X]=30.5
c
E[X]=81,Var[X]=33.6
d
E[X]=84,Var[X]=36.2
e
E[X]=84,Var[X]=33.6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic0,otherwise

Now, provided that N≫n, the random variables Xi can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have Xi∼Bernoulli(p)1≤i≤n where p is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable X, defined as X=∑i=1nXi can be approximated as a binomial random variable X≈B(n,p), where E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have p=60%=0.6,n=140.

Therefore, X≈B(140,0.6) and we have the following results for the mean and variance: E[X]=np=140⋅0.6=84Var[X]=np(1−p)=140⋅0.6⋅(1−0.6)=33.6

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ the random variables ${X}_{i}$ can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(p)\,1\le i\le n
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable $X,$ defined as 

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}
$$

can be approximated as a binomial random variable $X≈B(n,p),$ where

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have 

$$
p=60%=0.6,\,n=140.
$$

Therefore,

$$
X≈B(140,0.6)
$$

and we have the following results for the mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =140\cdot 0.6 \\  & =84 \\ \text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =140\cdot 0.6\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =33.6\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=140$ from a population where $60%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let the random variable ${X}_{i}$ be equal to

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic} \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

where $i=1,…,140.$ If the statistic $X$ is defined as

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{140}{X}_{i}
$$

find approximate values of $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{Var}[X].$

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Suppose that 60% of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of n=20 children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of right-handed children in the sample?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.024
b
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.012
c
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.012
d
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.024
e
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.018
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=60%=0.6, and n=20. Therefore, E[p^]=60%=0.6,Var[p^]=0.6(1−0.6)20=0.012.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*

Question 3
?

Suppose that 60% of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of n=20 children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of right-handed children in the sample?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.024
b
E[p^]=0.4,Var[p^]=0.012
c
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.012
d
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.024
e
E[p^]=0.6,Var[p^]=0.018
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=60%=0.6, and n=20. Therefore, E[p^]=60%=0.6,Var[p^]=0.6(1−0.6)20=0.012.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Suppose that $60%$ of the child population enrolled in a baseball academy is right-handed. A random sample of $n=20$ children is taken from the population and asked about their dominant hand.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of right-handed children in the sample? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=60%=0.6,$ and $n=20.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =60%=0.6, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.6(1-0.6)}{20} \\  & =0.012.\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Suppose that $25%$ of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of $n=25$ high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=25%=0.25,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =25%=0.25, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.25(1-0.25)}{25} \\  & =0.0075.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 4
?

Suppose that 25% of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of n=25 high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0065
b
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0085
c
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0065
d
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0075
e
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0075
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=25%=0.25, and n=25. Therefore, E[p^]=25%=0.25,Var[p^]=0.25(1−0.25)25=0.0075.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=25%=0.25,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =25%=0.25, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.25(1-0.25)}{25} \\  & =0.0075.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Suppose that $25%$ of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of $n=25$ high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*

question.html:
Question 4
?

Suppose that 25% of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of n=25 high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics?

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0065
b
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0085
c
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0065
d
E[p^]=0.25,Var[p^]=0.0075
e
E[p^]=0.75,Var[p^]=0.0075
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=25%=0.25, and n=25. Therefore, E[p^]=25%=0.25,Var[p^]=0.25(1−0.25)25=0.0075.

solution.reasoning: For a sample proportion with p=0.25 and n=25, the mean is p=0.25 and the variance is approximately p(1-p)/n=0.25(0.75)/25=0.0075. The large population justifies ignoring the finite-population correction. Thus option d is mathematically correct; no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Suppose that $25%$ of a high school student population like mathematics. A random sample of $n=25$ high school students is taken from the population and asked about their favorite subject.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of students in the sample who like mathematics? 

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=25%=0.25,$ and $n=25.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =25%=0.25, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.25(1-0.25)}{25} \\  & =0.0075.\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
It is known that  $5%$ of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of $n=15$ researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

It is known that 5% of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of n=15 researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to 4 decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0032
b
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0064
c
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0032
d
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0049
e
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0064
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=5%=0.05, and n=15. Therefore, E[p^]=5%=0.05,Var[p^]=0.05(1−0.05)15≈0.0032 rounded to 4 decimal places.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
It is known that  $5%$ of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of $n=15$ researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*

Question 5
?

It is known that 5% of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of n=15 researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of p^, the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to 4 decimal places where appropriate.

Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

a
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0032
b
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0064
c
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0032
d
E[p^]=0.05,Var[p^]=0.0049
e
E[p^]=0.95,Var[p^]=0.0064
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have a random sample of size n from a population of size N, and we define the sequence of random variables Xi as follows: Xi={1,ith member of the sample has the characteristic,0,otherwise.

Now, provided that N≫n, we have that X=∑i=1nXi≈B(n,p) where p is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and E[X]=np,Var[X]=np(1−p).

The sample proportion p^ is given by p^=X―=Xn.

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that E[p^]=p,Var[p^]=p(1−p)n.

In our case, we have p=5%=0.05, and n=15. Therefore, E[p^]=5%=0.05,Var[p^]=0.05(1−0.05)15≈0.0032 rounded to 4 decimal places.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
It is known that  $5%$ of the researchers in a particular university work in neurobiology. A random sample of $n=15$ researchers is taken from the population and asked about their work area.

What is the mean and variance of $\overset{^}{\,p},$ the proportion of researchers in the sample working in neurobiology? Round your answers to $4$ decimal places where appropriate.

*Hint: You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N,$ and we define the sequence of random variables ${X}_{i}$ as follows:

$$
{X}_{i}=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,i\text{th member of the sample has the characteristic}, \\ 0,\,\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, provided that $N≫n,$ we have that

$$
X={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}≈B(n,p)
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of the population that have the characteristic, and 

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,\,\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p).
$$

The sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ is given by

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}=\overset{―}{X}=\frac{X}{n}.
$$

Using the properties of expectation and variance, it is straightforward to show that

$$
\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=p,\,\text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}]=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.
$$

In our case, we have $p=5%=0.05,$ and $n=15.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =5%=0.05, \\ \text{Var}[\overset{^}{\,p}] & =\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{15} \\  & ≈0.0032\end{aligned}
